articles.title: Make an old, lumpy bed feel new again. Five mattress toppers that actually work
articles.summary: A topper can make a good mattress great, or change the feel of a mattress to your comfort level. After many nights of testing, we’ve found the best of the best. The best sleep masks and best Bluetooth sleep masks in the US.
body: I f you make your bed, you’ve gotta lie in it, but a mattress topper can help make it a more pleasant experience. These pads sit on top of the mattress, adding an extra layer that can fundamentally change the feel, making it firmer, softer or just helping to smooth out bumps and lumps. None of these products can fix an old and broken mattress: if the springs are shot or there is a dip in the mattress the shape of a long-dead relative, you may need a new mattress. But if you are stuck with a mattress that is too hard or too soft, adding a mattress topper can make it juuusssst right.

I’ve had nearly sixty years of experience in sleeping, and for over half of that, I’ve been testing consumer products ranging from automatic coffee makers to xBox peripherals for publications including PC World, Reviewed.com, CNET and many others. For all of those publications, I bring an objective scientific eye to testing products and helping consumers make better buying decisions.
After this review was completed, I donated all of the mattress toppers to furniture banks in Massachusetts that provide household goods to families in need.

articles.title: ‘You’re honoring a life well-lived’: embalmers describe their work (in great detail)
articles.summary: Embalming is one of the most common options for temporarily preserving bodies after death – but what exactly does it entail? Most people don’t like to think about what happens to people’s bodies after they die. Victoria Bilstein is an exception.
body: “I’ve actually wanted to be an embalmer since I was 10 years old!” says the funeral director, embalmer and author based in the midwest. As a child, Bilstein had two leg surgeries that incorporated bones from two deceased donors. After that, she wondered about the people who had helped save her life and the families who had lost them.

She saw this work as an opportunity to help grieving families. “I wanted to be able to do postmortem reconstruction on donors so their families had the option for a viewing,” she says. “It felt like such an amazing way to honor my donors.” In her six years in the industry, she estimates she’s worked on at least a thousand embalmings.
Most people who are planning burials and viewings for loved ones choose to have them embalmed.

But fewer and fewer American families are choosing burials. According to the National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA), the burial rate in 2025 was 31.6%, while the cremation rate was 63.4%. By 2045, the NFDA expects the cremation rate to reach 82.3%.

articles.title: The secret to a non-cloudy chicken stock | Kitchen aide
articles.summary: Don’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panel. Why is my chicken stock always cloudy? Ryan, by email From broths and risottos to sauces and braises, there’s no question that a good, flavourful stock will stand you in good stead.
body: Ryan’s clarity issue, Byatt says, is “only ever caused by cooking the stock too quickly or by allowing the fat to boil back into the base liquid”. So it’s crucial to take things low and slow. You will also need a pan that’s “big and heavy enough to give the bones enough room for movement, as well as a very fine sieve for straining the stock”.

On to the actual making, and Alissa Timoshkina, author of Lozhka, goes in cold. She puts chicken legs, drumsticks or a leftover roast chicken carcass in a large pot, adds her stock veg – onions, carrots, celery, garlic, say – and aromats (bay, parsley stalks, peppercorns, for instance), then covers the lot with cold water and brings everything very slowly to a boil. She then turns down the heat and leaves it to cook on a very gentle simmer. In the event of that carefully made stock going a bit cloudy, Timoshkina would seek to mollify that by straining the lot through a fine sieve and stirring in a tablespoon of lemon juice, which has the added benefit of being “great for flavour, too”.

articles.title: Where Will the Titular Girls of HBO’s ‘Girls’ Find Themselves 10 Years Later? Some Guesses
articles.summary: I can’t believe the wildly-to-mildly annoying young women who made me and my Brooklyn-dwelling friends feel a little too seen in 2018 are coming back for more.
body: I’m no Girls reboot writer, but hearing that the wildly-to-mildly annoying young women who made me and my Brooklyn-dwelling friends feel a little too seen in 2018 are returning to the small screen made me wonder what Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, and Jessa would be up to in 2026 (or, rather, 2027, as production is slated to begin next summer—a decade after the original series finale). Below, find my absolute best guesses.

Hey, remember that baby Hannah randomly had? Grover would be 10 or 11 years old in the reboot, and I’d love to see Hannah begin to navigate the highly competitive New York high school admissions process with him—though it’s totally possible that mother and son are still in small-town New York, where we left them in the season-six finale. Hear me out: Is it crazy to think that Hannah might actually be… professionally successful in the reboot, maybe balancing a burgeoning career as a single-mom memoirist and professor in upstate New York with always being at least 15 minutes late to pick up Grover from forest school?

articles.title: Inside Simu Liu and Allison Hsu’s Wedding at a 17th-Century Chateau in Provence
articles.summary: The actor Simu Liu married the music executive Allison Hsu in the South of France with a candlelit welcome party inside a former limestone quarry, a rain-dappled ceremony, and a surprise DJ set from ‘Shang-Chi’ star Benedict Wong. See all the exclusive photos here.
body: Actor, writer, and producer Simu Liu and Allison Hsu, the vice president of digital marketing at Interscope Records, first met in 2022 at a mutual friend’s Fourth of July barbecue. Whenever this comes up, “Simu likes to say ‘God, bless America,’” Allison jokes.

After nearly three years of dating, Simu proposed on May 10, 2025, on the rooftop of the Shangri-La Hotel in Paris, surprising Allison with a string quartet and a private dinner attended by her closest friends and family, who he had secretly flown in for the occasion.

For their recent early October wedding weekend, the couple returned to France, this time choosing Provence for a weekend-long celebration planned by Lisa Vorce. “From the moment that we saw Carrières des Lumières and Chateâu d’Estoubon in our initial search, we knew that the south of France would be the perfect location for our dream celebration,” Allison says. “[And after we chose the location,] it took the world’s most incredible village to help us execute our plans step by step. This was ultimately the greatest joy—planning not only as a couple but as an entire community with our friends and family, and our highly talented and generous team, led by Lisa.”

articles.title: The Return of Relaxer: Why Are Some Black Women Rethinking Their Natural Hair?
articles.summary: Ata-owaji Victor explores why, amid mounting lawsuits and potential health concerns, some Black women are choosing to relax their hair again.
body: Renowned hairstylist Charlotte Mensah, who recently celebrated 40 years in the hair industry, has observed a similar shift, much of which she puts down to natural-hair fatigue. “What I’m seeing is that some people are simply exhausted by the amount of time, products, and manipulation they’ve come to associate with maintaining natural hair,” she says. “Deep conditioning, layering multiple products, long wash days, and daily styling can become overwhelming.” But, she counters, “natural hair itself isn’t the problem. Often it’s the routine that has become too complicated. Hair care shouldn’t feel like a burden.”
So why, at a moment of unprecedented scrutiny, are some Black women going back?

Celebrity hairstylist Andree Marie, founder of London’s Andree Marie Salon, who has styled numerous celebrities including Tems and Burna Boy, believes there is no single answer. Trends matter—particularly the revival of short ’90s styles like the pixie cut seen recently on Zendaya —but so do the realities of everyday life.
